name: Sesame
summary: We buy sesame seed in Sudan, ship it to Saudi Arabia, remove the skin (hulling), and turn part of it into tahini and halawa. Leftovers become sesame oil and animal feed.

tree.name: Sesame: from Sudan to buyers

children.name: 1 · Growing & harvest (Sudan)
Planting with the first rains
children.t: Large mechanised farms in Gedaref and small family farms elsewhere.

children.name: Plants grow and fill their pods
children.t: If the rain stops in these months, the harvest is much smaller.

children.name: Cutting, drying and threshing
children.t: Plants are cut by hand, stacked to dry, then shaken to release the seed. Late harvesting loses seed on the ground.

children.name: White sesame
children.t: The type we want. Best for hulling, tahini and bread toppings.

children.name: Red / brown sesame
children.t: Mostly pressed for oil. Not suitable for hulling.

children.name: Mixed sesame
children.t: Cheaper. Used for oil and lower-quality products.

children.name: Gedaref
children.t: The main sesame market, where prices are set. In 2023/24 Gedaref and Sennar each grew about a quarter of Sudan's sesame.

children.name: Blue Nile & Sennar
children.t: Large rain-fed farms.

children.name: Kordofan
children.t: Small farms. Hard to reach because of the war.

children.name: White Nile
children.t: Smaller growing area.

children.name: About 626,000 tonnes in 2024
children.t: Official FAO figure. Down from a peak of 1.5 million tonnes in 2020. An industry estimate for 2025 is about 485,000 tonnes.

children.name: 320,000–390,000 tonnes expected in 2026
children.t: Rainfall in 2026 was 30% below average in Gedaref and 20% below in Sennar, the two main sesame states, so the harvest will be smaller.

children.name: About a quarter of world exports
children.t: Sudan is one of the world's top sesame exporters. China has historically bought about half.

children.name: About 289,000 tonnes exported in 2025
children.t: Worth $334 million, an average of about $1,155 per tonne (customs value, may be understated).

children.name: About half of Saudi Arabia's sesame imports
children.t: In 2023 Saudi Arabia imported about 48,100 tonnes of sesame worth $116 million. Sudan supplied 48%, ahead of India (20%), Pakistan and Brazil.
Sesame grows once a year in the rainy season. Farmers plant in summer and harvest in autumn.

children.name: 2 · Buying in Sudan
Farmers and farm schemes
children.t: Cheapest way to buy, but needs local agents, cash and careful quality checks.

children.name: Gedaref crop market
children.t: The main market where Sudanese sesame prices are set.

children.name: Sennar, El Obeid and Kosti
children.t: Smaller regional markets.

children.name: Awad Rabie Ibrahim & Sons
children.t: Based in Sennar. Sells under standard GAFTA contract rules with pre-shipment inspection.

children.name: Samasim Investment Group
children.t: Large exporter working between Sudan and the UAE.

children.name: Abnaa Sayed Elobeid
children.t: One of Sudan's major crop exporters.

children.name: Ethiopia (Humera area)
children.t: Same type of seed as Gedaref. The closest alternative.

children.name: Nigeria, Tanzania, Burkina Faso, Chad
children.t: Keep the factory running if Sudan supply stops.

children.name: India
children.t: Sets world prices. Also our main competitor for hulled sesame.

children.name: About $1,150–1,400 per tonne at Port Sudan
children.t: Central Bank export average was about $1,155 per tonne in 2025; African standard grades were about $1,400 FOB in October 2026. Premium white seed sells higher.
Most buying happens just after harvest, when quality is best. This is when the most cash is needed.

children.name: 3 · Cleaning & paperwork (Sudan)
Cleaning and grading
children.t: Done in the exporter's warehouse. 2–8% of the weight is lost as dust and stones.

children.name: Quality and plant-health certificates
children.t: SSMO quality certificate, phytosanitary certificate, certificate of origin, and pre-shipment inspection.

children.name: Export registration and payment rules
children.t: Sudan's central bank sets rules on how export money is returned. These change often, so check every season.
Before export, the seed is cleaned and the documents are prepared.

children.name: 4 · Shipping to Saudi Arabia
Truck to Port Sudan
children.t: 800–1,200 km, 3–10 days. Risks: fuel shortages, checkpoints and unofficial road charges.

children.name: Loading into containers
children.t: Sometimes fumigated against insects.

children.name: Ship to Jeddah or Jazan
children.t: Only 1–2 days at sea. About $60 per tonne. This short trip is a big advantage.
The seed travels by truck to Port Sudan, then by ship across the Red Sea.

children.name: 5 · Arriving in Saudi Arabia
Customs clearance (or bonded zone)
children.t: If the factory is in a bonded zone or SEZ, no import duty is paid on seed that is re-exported.

children.name: SFDA food-safety checks
children.t: Samples are tested for Salmonella, pesticide limits and aflatoxin.

children.name: Cost at our factory: about $1,400 per tonne
children.t: Landed cost: purchase price plus shipping, insurance, port fees and trucking.
Customs and food-safety checks before the seed reaches our factory.

children.name: 6 · Our factory: production lines
Line 1: Cleaning & hulling
Input: 1.22 tonnes of natural seed per tonne hulled
children.t: Yield is about 82%: some weight is lost as skins and broken seed.

children.name: Steps: sort → soak → remove skin → dry
children.t: Mechanical method, no chemicals. A colour sorter removes dark seeds.

children.name: Steam sterilisation
children.t: Kills bacteria. Needed to sell to Europe, Japan and big brands.

children.name: Main product: hulled sesame
children.t: Sells for about $2,100 per tonne. Indian EU-quality hulled seed was €1,850–1,890 per tonne FOB on 25 Oct 2026.

children.name: By-product: seed skins
children.t: About 0.15 tonnes per tonne of hulled seed. Sold to animal-feed makers or burned for fuel.

children.name: By-product: broken & dark seeds
children.t: Rejected by the colour sorter. Instead of being thrown away, they go to Line 4 to make oil.

children.name: Waste: stones and dust
children.t: No value. Small disposal cost.

children.name: Margin: about $240 per tonne
children.t: Sell at $2,100 minus seed ($1,707) and processing (~$150).
Capacity 1.5 tonnes per hour, about 5,000 tonnes of hulled seed a year. Machines and setup cost about $1.2–3.5 million (capex).

children.name: Line 2: Roasting & tahini
Input: 1.07 tonnes of hulled seed per tonne of tahini
children.t: Roasting dries the seed, so a little weight is lost.

children.name: Steps: roast → cool → grind → heat-treat
children.t: Seeds are ground between stones or steel discs into a smooth paste.

children.name: Main product: tahini
children.f: 200 kg drums, large tanks or jars
children.t: Bulk tahini sells for roughly $2,700–3,200 per tonne (estimate).

children.name: By-product: roasting dust
children.t: Small amount; goes to Line 4.

children.name: Margin: about $400–600 per tonne
children.t: Higher than hulling because the extra processing cost is small.
Takes part of the hulled sesame from Line 1.

children.name: Line 3: Halawa
Input: half tahini, half sugar
children.t: About 0.50 tonnes of tahini and 0.48 tonnes of sugar syrup per tonne, plus a natural foaming root extract and flavours.

children.name: Steps: cook syrup → mix → knead → mould → cool
Main product: halawa
children.f: 5 kg tubs or 250 g / 500 g jars
children.t: Bulk about $2,800–3,500 per tonne; supermarket own-brand about $3,500–4,500 per tonne.

children.name: By-product: trimmings
children.t: Edges and broken pieces are melted down and reused.

children.name: Margin: about $1,700 per tonne
children.t: Sales of about $3,500 minus costs of about $1,800, before shelf fees and marketing.
Cooking pots, mixers and moulds.

children.name: Line 4: Oil press (uses leftovers)
Input: broken seeds and roasting dust
Steps: press → filter
children.t: A screw press squeezes out the oil.

children.name: Main product: sesame oil
children.t: About 40–45% of the seed weight becomes oil. Used in cooking and cosmetics.

children.name: By-product: seed cake
children.t: What is left after pressing (about 55%). Protein-rich animal feed.

children.name: Margin: small but positive
children.t: Its main job is to turn waste into cash.
Turns leftovers from Lines 1 and 2 into money.
Each production line takes one input and makes one main product. Leftovers (by-products) are sold or used by another line.

children.name: 7 · What we sell & how it's packed
Hulled sesame (standard)
children.t: For bakeries and food factories in the Middle East.

children.name: Hulled sesame (EU quality)
children.t: Cleaner and tested. For Europe, the UK and Japan.

children.name: Tahini in bulk
children.t: For hummus makers, restaurants and halawa makers.

children.name: Tahini in jars (supermarket brand)
children.t: Private label for supermarkets.

children.name: Halawa in bulk
children.t: For sweet shops, bakeries and export.

children.name: Halawa in jars (supermarket brand)
children.t: Private label for supermarkets.

children.name: Animal-feed leftovers
children.t: Seed skins and seed cake.
Finished products ready for customers.

children.name: 8 · Who buys it & where
Bakeries and burger-bun makers
children.t: Buy every day for sesame-topped bread.

children.name: Halwani Bros and Al-Jameel
children.t: Large tahini and halawa makers. Possible customers and also competitors.

children.name: Supermarkets (Panda, Tamimi, Danube, Lulu)
children.f: halawa and tahini under their own brand
children.t: Private label. They usually charge fees for shelf space.

children.name: Restaurants and caterers
children.t: Hummus, shawarma and salad sauces.

children.name: Animal-feed makers and dairy farms
children.t: Saudi Arabia imports a lot of animal feed, so local supply is welcome.

children.name: UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain
children.t: 2–7 days by truck. No import duty if the product counts as Saudi origin.

children.name: Jordan, Lebanon, Iraq, Yemen
children.t: People here eat a lot of tahini and halawa. Arab free-trade rules lower duties.

children.name: Germany, Greece, UK, Netherlands
children.t: Pay well but demand BRCGS certification and strict pesticide limits.

children.name: China
children.t: The biggest buyer in the world. Very price-focused. Exporters must register with Chinese customs.

children.name: Japan and South Korea
children.f: hulled seed; natural seed for oil
children.t: High prices but very strict testing.

children.name: USA and Canada
children.t: US food-import rules apply; sesame must be labelled as an allergen.

children.name: East Africa and aid agencies
children.t: Price-sensitive buyers.
Customers, where they are, and what form they buy.

children.name: 9 · Money: margins & profit
Halawa earns about $800–1,200 per tonne
children.t: Lowered in Oct 2026: Halwani Bros, the Saudi market leader, made a 28.6% gross margin in 2025. 28–35% of a $2,800–3,500 selling price is about $800–1,200.

children.name: Oil and seed cake earn a little
Break-even: about 3,000 tonnes hulled a year
children.t: Assumes about $600,000 a year of fixed costs (staff, rent, certificates, sales).

children.name: Profit from hulling only: about $165,000 a year
children.t: Base case at 5,000 tonnes. In a bad year this becomes a loss.

children.name: Profit with 1,000 tonnes of halawa: about $0.8–1.2 million a year
children.t: Halawa brings most of the profit.
How much each line earns. Click an item to jump to its production line.

children.name: 10 · Rules & risks
Salmonella after hulling
children.t: Once the skin is off, seed is easier to contaminate. Test every batch and use steam sterilisation.

children.name: Farm-chemical residues (Europe)
children.t: In 2020 the EU recalled large amounts of Indian sesame because of a banned chemical (ethylene oxide).

children.name: Extra EU border checks
children.t: In 2026 the EU rejected 11 Sudanese sesame shipments because health certificates were missing.

children.name: Saudi licences and certificates
children.t: SFDA factory licence, Halal, and FSSC 22000 or BRCGS.

children.name: War in Sudan and sudden rule changes
children.t: Use backup origins and keep safety stock.

children.name: Competitor: Halwani Bros (Tadawul 6001)
children.t: Saudi market leader in halawa. Revenue SAR 904 million in 2025.

children.name: Competitor: Haitoglou (Greece)
children.t: One of the world's largest sesame processors, about 150 tonnes a day.

children.name: Competitor: Al Jameel International Trading
children.t: One of the largest importers of hulled sesame into Saudi Arabia; supplies bakeries and food factories.

children.name: Competitors: local tahini and halawa factories
children.t: Smaller Saudi makers such as Al Jabal (Dammam, since 1996), Al Muna (Riyadh) and Rahash (wholesale tahini and halawa) compete on price in bulk and food-service packs.

children.name: Imported brands on Saudi shelves
children.t: Al Wadi Al Akhdar (Lebanon), Haitoglou (Greece) and Turkish brands compete in supermarkets.
What can go wrong and which rules must be followed.

tree.t: Follow the stages from left to right. They are in time order, from the farm in Sudan to the final buyer.

name: Gum Arabic
summary: Gum arabic is a natural gum collected from Acacia trees. We would crush it, dissolve it, clean it and dry it into a fine powder that soft-drink, sweet and medicine makers use.

tree.name: Gum arabic: from Sudan to buyers

children.name: 1 · Tapping & collecting (Sudan)
Cutting the tree bark
children.t: Done after the rainy season ends.

children.name: Picking the dried lumps
children.t: Picked several times, every 2–3 weeks.

children.name: Hashab (best quality)
children.t: From the Acacia senegal tree. The best emulsifier for soft drinks.

children.name: Talha (cheaper)
children.t: From the Acacia seyal tree. Used for fibre products and sweets.

children.name: North & South Kordofan
children.t: Main Hashab area. Badly affected by the war.

children.name: Darfur
children.t: Hard to access due to the war.

children.name: Blue Nile, White Nile, Gedaref, Sennar
children.t: Eastern areas, easier to reach.

children.name: Exports fell about 60% after the war started
children.t: According to Sudan's Gum Arabic Exporters' Association (2025).

children.name: World market: about 120,000 tonnes, $1.1 billion a year
children.t: Estimate cited by Kerry Group.

children.name: About 62,500 tonnes exported in 2025
children.t: Up from about 48,000 tonnes in 2023/24, but still below 100,000–150,000 tonnes before the war. Customs value $78 million.

children.name: Saudi Arabia buys very little gum arabic
children.t: Only about 343 tonnes ($1.5 million) were imported in 2023, mostly from China and Sudan. A Saudi gum factory must export most of its output to Europe, the US or Asia.
Workers cut the bark of Acacia trees; the gum oozes out and dries into lumps that are picked by hand.

children.name: Al-Obeid gum auction
children.t: Main Hashab market. Hard to reach because of the war.

children.name: Dar Savanna
children.t: Processor inside Sudan; check whether it is still operating.

children.name: Nigeria
children.t: Prices FOB Lagos in March 2026: cleaned $2,500–3,200, crushed $2,000–2,800, powder $3,000–4,000 per tonne.

children.name: About $2,500–5,000 per tonne (cleaned Hashab, sources disagree)
children.t: PAX for Peace reports Hashab rising from $2,200 before the war to $4,000–5,000. Nigerian cleaned gum was $2,500–3,200. The 2025 customs average for all grades was only about $1,250. Get real quotes.

children.name: Hand-sorting into grades
children.f: best lumps, cleaned, small pieces, dust
children.t: The best hand-picked lumps get the highest price.

children.name: Small pieces and dust
children.t: Lower grades sold for industrial uses.

children.name: Certificates and traceability file
children.t: Buyers ask for proof the gum does not come from conflict-controlled areas.

children.name: Truck to Port Sudan
children.t: Unofficial road charges of over 1 million Sudanese pounds per truck have been reported.

children.name: Ship to Jeddah
children.t: 1–2 days at sea.

children.name: Bonded zone or SEZ
children.t: Avoids import duty on gum that is re-exported.

children.name: Cost at our factory: about $2,900 per tonne
children.t: Example landed cost.

children.name: Line 1: Sorting & crushing
Input: 1.05 tonnes of lumps per tonne crushed
Steps: sort → crush → sieve
children.t: This crushing is called kibbling.

children.name: Main product: crushed gum
children.t: Sold as it is, or sent to Line 2.

children.name: By-product: fine dust
children.t: About 5%. Sold as industrial-grade gum.
Simple, low-cost first step.

children.name: Line 2: Dissolving & spray-drying
Input: 1.2 tonnes crushed gum per tonne of powder
children.t: Some weight is lost as bark, sand and water.

children.name: Steps: dissolve in water → filter → heat-treat
Steps: spray-dry → make granules
children.t: Granules dissolve faster for drink makers.

children.name: Main product: gum arabic powder (E414)
children.t: Drink-grade powder sells for roughly $5,000–7,000 per tonne (estimate). Lower-grade powder from Nigeria is $3,000–4,000.

children.name: By-product: bark and sand sludge
children.t: The insolubles filtered out of the gum.

children.name: Margin: about $1,000–2,000 per tonne
children.t: Depends on quality and energy costs.
The main value-adding line. Expensive machines and high energy use.

children.name: Steps: mix to exact recipes; medicine rules (GMP)
Main product: fibre and medicine-grade gum
children.t: Highest price, but needs special certificates.

children.name: 7 · What we sell & how it's packed
Industrial grade (dust, off-spec)
children.t: For glues, inks and printing.

children.name: Bark and sand waste
children.t: Composted or sent to landfill.

children.name: Soft-drink bottlers and flavour companies
children.t: Nobody makes gum powder in the Gulf today, so local supply is an advantage.

children.name: Nexira and Alland & Robert (France)
children.t: The world's biggest gum processors. Also competitors.

children.name: Fibre and medicine grade earn the most
The spray-dryer is the biggest cost
children.t: Get quotes from machine makers. Energy is a large running cost.

children.name: Proving the gum is not from conflict areas
children.t: Armed groups have been accused of smuggling gum. Check every supplier and keep traceability records.

children.name: Food-additive quality standards
children.t: Must meet the official E414 rules for food use.

children.name: Most supply is in war zones
children.t: The biggest risk for this crop.

tree.t: Sudan has supplied 70–80% of the world's gum arabic. Follow the stages left to right.

name: Baobab
summary: Baobab fruit grows wild in Sudan. We would grind the dry fruit pulp into a powder sold as a healthy food, press the seeds for cosmetic oil, and sell the rest as animal feed.

tree.name: Baobab: from Sudan to buyers

children.name: 1 · Wild harvest (Sudan)
Amount varies every year
children.t: Wild trees, no plantations, so supply is hard to predict.
Collected in the dry season by local people.

children.name: Rural markets (El Obeid, Nyala, En Nahud)
Omdurman wholesale market
children.t: Traditional Tabaldi trade; check if it is operating.

children.name: About $600–1,200 per tonne
children.t: For pulp with seeds, shell already removed. Raw baobab fruit sells for about $400–650 per tonne in African markets (2025 market report). No official Sudan price; ask exporters in El Obeid and Omdurman.

children.name: Shells
children.t: Used locally as fuel.

children.name: Drying in the sun and bagging
SFDA tests for bacteria and moisture
Cost at our factory: about $1,000–1,400 per tonne
children.t: Estimate.

children.name: Input: about 2 tonnes of pulp-with-seeds per tonne of powder
children.t: Seeds are about 40% and fibre about 10% of the weight (estimate).

children.name: Steps: separate seeds → grind → sieve → heat-treat
Main product: baobab fruit powder
children.t: Normal powder about $3–5 per kg; organic in Europe about $6–9 per kg (estimates).

children.name: By-product: seeds
children.t: About 0.8 tonnes per tonne of powder.

children.name: Margin: about $800–1,500 per tonne
children.t: Organic certification raises it.

children.name: Input: baobab seeds
children.t: About 10% of the seed weight becomes oil.

children.name: Main product: baobab seed oil
children.t: Used in skin and hair products. About $10–20 per kg (estimate).

children.name: By-product: seed cake
children.t: About 90% of the seed weight.

children.name: Main product: Tabaldi drink concentrate
children.t: Popular with Sudanese living in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf, especially in Ramadan.

children.name: Main product: smoothie and cereal mixes
7 · What we sell & how it's packed
UK and EU health-food brands
children.t: Approved as a Novel Food in the EU since 2008.

children.name: US health-food brands
children.t: Approved as a safe food ingredient in the US.

children.name: Prices change a lot; little public data
children.t: Get at least 3 buyer quotes before planning.

tree.t: Baobab trees are wild, not farmed. The fruit dries on the tree.

name: Hibiscus
summary: Hibiscus (Karkade) is a red flower dried to make a sour red drink. We would clean and cut it for tea companies, make syrups and natural red colouring from the small pieces, and sell drinks in the Gulf.

tree.name: Hibiscus (Karkade): from Sudan to buyers

children.name: 1 · Growing & harvest (Sudan)
Picking the red flower parts by hand
Drying in the sun
children.t: Dust and mould can be a problem.

children.name: Small family farms, often run by women

children.t: Grown by small farmers in the rainy season.

children.name: El Obeid, En Nahud and Nyala markets
About $1,500–2,300 per tonne
children.t: Lowered in Oct 2026. Dried calyces were about $1,450–1,900 per tonne FOB in early 2026; import prices into Mexico were about $1.80–3.47 per kg in 2024. No official Sudan price exists; ask exporters.

children.name: Remove seeds and stems; sort by colour
Seeds
children.t: Left in Sudan, or shipped for Line 4.

children.name: Export certificates
children.t: Phytosanitary certificate, SSMO, certificate of origin.

children.name: Ship to Jeddah
children.t: Hibiscus is light and bulky, so bigger containers help.

children.name: Tests for farm chemicals and bacteria
Cost at our factory: about $2,100–2,900 per tonne
children.t: Buying price plus about $600 for transport, port fees and checks (estimate).

children.name: Input: 1.15 tonnes of whole flowers per tonne of tea-bag cut
Main product: tea-bag cut hibiscus
children.t: About $3,500–5,000 per tonne (estimate).

children.name: By-product: small pieces and powder
children.t: About 10% of the weight.

children.name: Input: small pieces and lower-grade flowers
Steps: soak in hot water → filter → boil down
Spray-dry with gum arabic
children.t: Gum arabic helps turn the liquid into powder. This links to the Gum Arabic map.

children.name: Main product: extract powder and natural red colour
children.t: Priced by how much natural red colour (anthocyanin) it contains. Much higher price per kg.

children.name: Line 3: Drinks & tea bags (with a partner factory)
Main product: bottled drinks and Ramadan packs
Saudi tax on sweetened drinks
children.t: Sweetened drinks pay excise tax, which raises the shelf price.

children.name: 7 · What we sell & how it's packed
Bottled drinks, Ramadan packs, tea bags
German tea companies (e.g. Martin Bauer)
children.t: Historically bought most of Sudan's hibiscus. A trade guide calls Martin Bauer the largest single buyer of Sudanese hibiscus; US buyers often buy it through Germany.

children.name: Mexico (for 'agua de Jamaica' drink)
children.t: Imports over 15,000 tonnes a year.

children.name: Tea-bag cut earns about $600–1,000 per tonne
Extract earns a lot per tonne
children.t: Extract powder sells for about $30–38 per kg in trade data and costs about $12.50–18.20 per kg to make, so the margin per tonne is high, but volumes are small. Not yet checked with real quotes.

children.name: Sales peak before Ramadan
children.t: Plan stock and cash for this.

children.name: EU limits on farm chemicals and bacteria
Small volumes; war in Darfur and Kordofan

tree.t: Sudan's dark-red hibiscus is known as one of the best in the world.
